primary_sources.role: Cited in-article as an example of a cruise line publishing its own wave-season guide - used to support the claim that the lines themselves describe the period, not as a neutral authority.

claims.definition: Wave season as the industry's peak booking window running broadly January through March, with promotions for sailings roughly six to eighteen months out, and the origin as a push into the flat post-holiday weeks. Consistent across multiple sources checked 2026-09-05 including cruise lines' own guides. Stated with 'broadly' and 'roughly' because published date ranges vary slightly by source.
claims.NOT_claimed_deliberately: The article makes NO claim that wave season pricing is cheaper, or not cheaper, than any other month. It states explicitly in its own text that we have not tracked fares over time, have not compared across months and lines, and will not assert what we have not measured - and invites the reader to ask of any source whether it measured or repeated. This was the honest resolution of a topic where the obvious claims are unverifiable without price data we do not have.
claims.method_not_data: The value offered is an evaluation method (reduce every offer to all-in cost per night; value inclusions only at what you would have spent anyway) rather than assertions about market pricing. The method is sound regardless of whether wave pricing is favourable.
claims.conflict_disclosure: The article names that most wave-season content is published by parties who earn on booking, and states the site's own position (no money from cruise lines or travel agents) as the reason it can be indifferent to whether the reader books.

seasonal_note: Published 2026-09-05 deliberately ahead of the January-March window so it has time to rank before readers need it.
